name: PT Bangun Kosambi Sukses Tbk

frontmatter.title: Bangun Kosambi Sukses: the land is worth more than its carrying cost
frontmatter.summary: Revision. The audited segment note shows commercial land plots sold at a large multiple of their carrying cost, so the RNAV marks the land at a market value with the property method card haircuts rather than at book. We now share that mark-up with the minorities that own part of the land-holding subsidiaries, which cuts the RNAV and the target: HOLD at Rp2,816.
thesis: The land bank is carried at historical cost, but the audited segment note shows commercial land plots sold at several times their carrying cost, with a gross margin in the mid-eighties in FY2025 after a margin in the low sixties in FY2024; marking the land at a market value with the method card haircuts, and sharing the mark-up with the minorities that own part of the land-holding companies, brings the discounted RNAV to roughly the share price rather than far below it.

At Rp2,730 the market capitalises the equity below audited book plus the land revaluation the segment margins support; the shares trade above book on a premium to the peer median, and the premium is justified by the land rather than by earnings.

The profit and loss account runs on a customer-advance book, not on current sales: FY2025 revenue of IDR2,503.6bn compares with marketing sales of IDR430.2bn, so revenue normalises as the backlog unwinds unless a bulk transaction lands.

Management set a FY2025 marketing-sales target of IDR2,030.0bn and delivered IDR430.2bn, about a fifth of it, after cutting the target to IDR508.0bn; that history is the strongest argument against extrapolating the land value into a near-term earnings recovery.

Downside is cushioned by cash of IDR3,636.8bn against bank loans of IDR42.5bn current and IDR159.3bn non-current, no material foreign-currency debt, and a controlling shareholder with every incentive to keep the township funded.

blocks.text: We move to **HOLD** on PT Bangun Kosambi Sukses with a twelve-month target of **Rp2,816**, a total return of **4.4%** from the Rp2,730 price. The previous SELL rested on an RNAV that marked a large land bank at just below its audited carrying cost. That was wrong, and the review was right to challenge it: the audited segment note shows the commercial-land-plot business earned revenue of IDR1,167.8bn on cost of revenue of IDR175.0bn in FY2025, and IDR1,083.4bn on IDR395.3bn in FY2024 [S3 p.102], so realised sale prices are a multiple of the carrying cost of the plots sold and inventory is not a ceiling on value. [S3 p.102, p.393]

The revised RNAV derives a market land value from those realised margins, applies the property method card's haircut band by land status, and only then applies the target discount to RNAV. Because the land sits in project companies the group owns roughly three quarters to four fifths of, the mark-up is shared with the minority holders before it reaches the parent: we deduct the minorities' share of the revaluation, a little over a fifth of it, from the land block, leaving an undiscounted RNAV per share above the market price before the discount is applied. Sharing the mark-up the parent does not own, rather than deducting only the book minority interest, is what the previous version of this note got wrong. It produces an RNAV method value of Rp2,676 per share at a 42.0% discount, against Rp1,200 on P/BV and Rp3,441 on P/E, blended at the weights shown in the valuation table and rolled forward at our cost of equity of 11.9% net of the next-twelve-month dividend of Rp34. The probability-weighted scenario value is Rp2,816 and, with no liquidity discount applied, the final target is Rp2,816. [S3 p.408, S6, S0]

The variant view is about the asset, not the earnings. At Rp2,730 the market capitalises the equity below audited book plus the land revaluation the segment margins support, and the shares sit at 1.4x P/BV on the 30 September 2026 book against a peer median of 0.6x: the premium over peer book is only defensible if the land is worth well above carrying cost, which is what the segment note shows. What keeps the call at HOLD rather than BUY is the operating evidence. Marketing sales of IDR430.2bn in FY2025 were about a fifth of the IDR2,030.0bn target the company had set a year earlier [S5 p.28, S3 p.35, p.46]; IDR448.0bn in the first nine months of FY2026 is still small against the revenue base [S2]; and the land bank turns at a few hectares a year, so the market-value mark is a statement about the asset, not about when it converts. [S3, S2]

What would move the value further: a bulk commercial-land transaction at the FY2024 scale, the next independent appraisal being published rather than merely referenced, marketing sales above the IDR563.1bn target for successive quarters, or a rate path that revives plot demand. Against that, a wider RNAV discount, a land correction, or a dilutive free-float placement would take the target back toward the price. [S3, S2, S7]

CBDK is a property developer focused on the Central Business District of the Pantai Indah Kapuk Dua township in Tangerang, Banten, on the northern coast of Greater Jakarta. The company listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange in January 2025 and is controlled by PT Pantai Indah Kapuk Dua Tbk, itself part of the Agung Sedayu and Salim group sphere, which together hold a large majority of the shares [S3, S4]. The business is best understood as a township land monetisation story with a small and growing recurring-income arm, rather than as a conventional residential developer with a broad product pipeline. [S3]

The development segment is the whole of the economics today. In FY2025, development revenue was IDR2,420.6bn out of total revenue of IDR2,503.6bn, while rental and other recurring revenue was IDR35.5bn [S3]. Within development, commercial land plots dominate: they contributed the large majority of the first nine months of FY2026 revenue, with commercial products such as SOHO The Bund, Bizpark and Rukan Pasar Milenial and residential products such as Rumah Milenial and Permata Hijau Residence making up the balance [S4, S2]. The sale of raw or semi-finished plots carries almost no construction cost, which is why the group gross margin reaches 66.0% and the EBITDA margin 57.5%. [S3, S0]

The land bank is the asset that matters. The company reports 702 ha of land reserves, most of it inside the township, carried on two balance-sheet lines that total IDR7,087.2bn of current inventory and IDR6,768.8bn of undeveloped land at 30 September 2026 [S6 p.2, S3 p.393-394]. The annual note splits the current line into land and buildings ready for sale of IDR871.5bn, buildings under construction of IDR424.3bn and land under development of IDR5,613.7bn [S3 p.393]. The strategy is to accelerate the use of productive land, continue building township infrastructure, and add commercial and residential products that fit the demand it sees from businesses wanting an address in the district [S3]. That strategy is capital-light in the development segment because buyers prepay: customer advances stood at IDR9,546.8bn at the end of FY2025 and IDR6,794.9bn current plus IDR1,138.8bn non-current nine months later, which funds infrastructure without bank debt. [S3, S6]

The 2025 capital increases into the two project companies are disclosed and were fairness-reviewed, but they do not corroborate a market-value mark. The company injected IDR2,000.9bn into PT Mega Andalan Sukses on 24 December 2025 and IDR91.7bn into PT Cahaya Gemilang Indah Cemerlang in June, both reviewed against an independent appraisal of the property's market value by KJPP Suwendho Rinaldy & Rekan [S3 p.138-143]. The December MAS subscription bought a fifth of the enlarged capital, not the small net ownership step the headline suggests: most of the new capital went to the parent, and the published percentage-point change in its stake is what is left after its existing holding is diluted by the new shares, so the headline understates the size of the subscription and overstates the price paid per point of ownership [S3 p.408]. On that reading the transaction prices MAS at about its book value and a fraction of its IDR10,460.5bn of total assets, so it is evidence about process and related-party pricing, not about the market value of land; we do not use it to support the mark. The appraised figures themselves are named but not quantified. [S3 p.138-143, p.362, p.408]

The recurring-income arm is small but strategically important. CBDK owns the Nusantara International Convention Exhibition, or NICE, acquired in January 2025 with proceeds from the listing, and describes it as the largest convention and exhibition centre in Jakarta and its surroundings [S3]. NICE has hosted a steady calendar of events including the Java Jazz Festival and Hyrox, and the company is building the Hilton PIK Dua, a five-star hotel targeted to open in the second half of 2027 [S2]. Rental revenue of IDR35.5bn is still trivial against the development line, but it is the part of the business that could eventually cover fixed costs through a property downcycle. [S3]

On competitive position, CBDK is not a volume leader among Indonesian developers. It is a township specialist with a single master plan, competing for corporate and retail buyers against other Greater Jakarta satellite townships and against the broader estate of its parent. Its advantage is location and infrastructure: the partial opening of the KATARAJA toll road section that connects the area to Soekarno-Hatta airport and the wider Jabodetabek network has improved access, and third-party facilities such as bank buildings and the Beachwalk lifestyle centre have made the district more usable [S2]. Its disadvantage is concentration: one township, one controlling shareholder, and a land supply that comes from the master plan of the parent. [S3, S2]

The group structure is straightforward but concentrated. PT Pantai Indah Kapuk Dua is the controlling shareholder with a stake above four-fifths of the shares, the public holds the remainder, and the President Commissioner, Richard Halim Kusuma, is disclosed as the ultimate beneficial owner [S3]. The President Director is Steven Kusumo [S2]. The group employs 161.0 people directly, which underlines how much of the development work is contracted out and how small the fixed cost base is. [S0]

The Indonesian property market entered 2026 in a gradual recovery rather than a boom. The review of the company describes national residential sales rising slightly year on year in 2025 but accelerating sharply on a quarterly basis in the final quarter, citing Bank Indonesia data, and points to government incentives, easier permitting and middle-class purchasing power as the policy supports for the sector [S3]. Gross domestic product growth remained in the mid single digits, household consumption was solid, and the rupiah and interest rates were described as stable [S3]. For a developer selling commercial plots to businesses, that backdrop is supportive but not transformative: demand tracks business formation and confidence more than it tracks household mortgage rates. [S3]

The macro driver that matters most for CBDK is the interest-rate path, because it sets both the cost of funding for the buyer and the capitalisation rate applied to the recurring assets. Our macro deck carries Bank Indonesia policy at 5.8% through the forecast and inflation near 3.3%, with real growth around 5.3%; we use a cost of equity of 11.9% and a cap rate of 8.5% for the income assets [S0]. The company itself lists global geopolitical tension, rupiah volatility, inflation and interest rates as the external risks it monitors, which is consistent with a business whose buyers are small and medium enterprises with financing needs. [S3, S2]

Regulation cuts two ways. On the supportive side, the government agenda of incentives and easier permitting for housing and property is explicitly cited by the company as a growth driver, and a VAT exemption or a continuation of the non-collected VAT treatment for housing would help demand for plots and products [S3]. On the constraining side, the affiliated-transaction regime under the capital-market rules governs how the company buys land and services from its parent, and the annual report devotes a section to compliance with those rules [S3]. For an investor, the practical question is whether the transfer pricing between the parent and the listed entity is fair; the 2025 capital increases were fairness-reviewed off an independent appraisal, which supports the company's arm's-length claim, although the appraised figures themselves are not published. [S3 p.138-143]

Demand for the specific product CBDK sells is narrower than headline residential statistics suggest. Commercial land plots in a master-planned district are bought by businesses that want a branded address, by investors anticipating further infrastructure, and by operators who will build on the plot. That demand is lumpy and relationship-driven: the FY2024 marketing sales figure of IDR2,120.0bn against IDR430.2bn in FY2025 shows how one or two large transactions can dominate a year [S5, S3]. The first nine months of FY2026, at IDR448.0bn, were up strongly on the prior year but still small relative to the revenue being recognised, which tells us the bulk market has not yet returned. [S2]

On the five forces, buyer power is high because corporate plot buyers are few and can wait; supplier power is high because the land comes from the master plan of the controlling shareholder rather than an open market; the threat of substitutes is meaningful because Greater Jakarta has several competing satellite townships and office districts; rivalry is moderate because each township is differentiated by location and infrastructure; and the threat of new entrants is low at the township scale, since assembling and permitting a comparable land position takes years. The moat, in other words, is the land position and the infrastructure already sunk into it, not the brand or the sales machine. [S3, S2]

The competitive landscape is best framed by the parent. Pantai Indah Kapuk Dua is itself listed and trades at a premium P/BV to the developer sector, reflecting the appetite of the market for the township story rather than for its reported earnings [S0]. CBDK is the CBD arm of that township, which gives it a reflected premium and a reflected dependency: the master plan of the parent determines access, amenities and the sequencing of land release, and the capital needs of the parent can influence how the listed subsidiary is run. That is a structural feature of the investment case, not a temporary one. [S3, S0]

External influences beyond rates are limited but not absent. The company has no material foreign-currency debt, so rupiah moves affect buyer sentiment rather than the balance sheet [S0]. Commodity input costs matter less than for a builder because the product is land, and construction of township infrastructure is contracted. The main external swing factor is therefore confidence: a recession that freezes corporate plot purchases would hit marketing sales before it hit reported revenue, because revenue is protected by the advance book for a period. [S3]

The reported history is one of rapid growth in revenue and profit, driven by land handovers. Revenue rose from IDR1,953.5bn in FY2023 to IDR2,249.0bn in FY2024 and IDR2,503.6bn in FY2025, with gross profit of IDR1,653.6bn and EBITDA of IDR1,438.4bn in the last year [S0, S3]. Net profit attributable to owners was IDR578.5bn, IDR924.8bn and IDR1,360.0bn across the three years, and earnings per share reached Rp240 in FY2025 [S0]. The margins are extraordinary by developer standards, with a gross margin of 66.0%, an EBITDA margin of 57.5% and a net margin of 54.3%, and they are explained by the product: land plots sold with little or no construction cost attached. [S0, S3]

Our forecast continues the growth but at a decelerating rate. We model revenue of IDR2,855.5bn in FY2026, IDR3,215.4bn in FY2027 and IDR3,441.7bn in FY2028, with EBITDA of IDR1,997.1bn, IDR2,152.2bn and IDR2,201.0bn and attributable net profit of IDR1,915.1bn, IDR2,166.4bn and IDR2,338.3bn [S0]. The revenue build uses a total-sales-value line, not the marketing-sales KPI: the line that feeds it is the sales value recognised at handover, the only measure that reproduces reported revenue, while marketing sales were IDR430.2bn in FY2025 and IDR448.0bn in nine months of FY2026 [S3, S2]. We label it that way because feeding the KPI into a revenue formula would collapse the forecast, and because the two measures answer different questions: the KPI is new contracts, the revenue line is handover value. The development gross margin is held near the nine-month level, fading only slowly as built products take a larger share; operating costs are held at the FY2025 actual of 8.9% of revenue rather than at a three-year average, because the cost base is largely fixed and nothing in the accounts shows it falling. [S3, S0]

Actual against forecast is now a one-quarter question. The interim LK to 30 September 2026 reports revenue of IDR2,557.7bn, cost of revenue of IDR519.6bn, gross profit of IDR2,038.0bn, final tax of IDR84.6bn and profit attributable to owners of IDR1,823.9bn [S6 p.5]. Our FY2026 forecast is revenue of IDR2,855.5bn and attributable profit of IDR1,915.1bn, so the nine months have already delivered most of the revenue and nearly all of the profit, and a fourth quarter in line with the third gets us there [S0]. The quarterly shape is the point: the third quarter contributed a small fraction of the nine-month revenue with a visibly lower gross margin than the first half, as handovers of built product replaced land lots [S0]. We carry the FY2026 development gross margin at 79.0%, in line with the nine-month actual rather than below it, and fade it to 67.0% by FY2030 and to the FY2025 audited level in perpetuity, because the residential and commercial-product segments earn margins far below the land lots and take share again as the land-lot pipeline is sold [S6, S3 p.101].

The guidance history is the strongest evidence on demand durability. The FY2024 annual report set a FY2025 marketing-sales target of IDR2,030.0bn [S5 p.28]; the FY2025 report restates the target at IDR508.0bn [S3 p.35]; actual sales were IDR430.2bn, about a fifth of the original plan and most of the revised one [S3 p.46]. A plan cut by three quarters within a year means the IDR563.1bn FY2026 target should be treated as an aspiration rather than a forecast, and that a bulk transaction, not the retail plot market, is what moves the year. [S3, S5]

Two limits on the forecast are stated plainly: the model's presales line is a handover-revenue proxy, so it cannot reproduce an advance book of IDR6,794.9bn current plus IDR1,138.8bn non-current that turns only about once every four years [S3 p.400, S6]; and the bulk commercial-land line is not evidenced by the marketing-sales KPI, which was IDR430.2bn in FY2025 and IDR448.0bn in 9M2026 [S3, S2]. We therefore treat the IDR563.1bn FY2026 marketing-sales target and the conversion of the advance book as the kill criteria for the base case, not as decoration (see the risks and monitoring sections). The revenue path without the bulk line is shown as the bear case: marketing sales alone support revenue nearer the marketing-sales figure than the revenue base, which is why the bear marks the land down as well. [S3, S2]

Working capital is the defining feature of the cash flow, and the arithmetic matters. Collections on outstanding contracts in a period equal revenue less the change in advances, so the FY2025 fall in the advance book alongside a full year of revenue implies collections several times the marketing-sales KPI: the gap is instalments on contracts signed in earlier years, not new contracts, because the KPI records new sales only. Customer advances of IDR9,546.8bn at the end of FY2025 exceeded annual revenue; nine months later they are IDR6,794.9bn current plus IDR1,138.8bn non-current, still larger than annual revenue but lower because handovers consumed the book [S6]. Net working capital was IDR-1,226.2bn in FY2025, which means the business releases cash as it sells rather than consuming it [S3, S0]. Free cash flow to the firm was IDR1,390.4bn in FY2025 and IDR4,976.0bn in FY2024, well above reported net profit in the earlier year because of the advance inflow [S0]. Capex was IDR163.9bn in FY2025, about 6.5% of revenue, directed at township infrastructure, NICE and the Hilton build [S0, S3]. The nine months to September have already spent more than the whole of FY2025 on the same programme, which is why we model capex at 7.8% of revenue in FY2026 before it steps back [S0, S6].

The balance sheet is conservative in the way that matters. At 30 September 2026 the company held cash of IDR3,636.8bn against bank loans of IDR42.5bn current and IDR159.3bn non-current, a net cash position several times the entire debt, and equity attributable to owners of IDR10,678.8bn within total equity of IDR13,717.4bn [S6 p.2-p.4]. In FY2025 interest income of IDR253.9bn exceeded interest expense of IDR25.6bn several times over, so the company is a net receiver of interest, not a payer, and there is no unhedged foreign-currency debt worth the name [S0]. Book value per share was Rp1,592 at the last year end. The minority balance is large because several project companies are only partly owned, and that is why our valuation deducts minorities from RNAV. [S0, S6]

The tax line is the main earnings-quality question. The income tax charge in the data pack was IDR49.1bn on pre-tax profit of IDR1,516.4bn, an effective rate far below the statutory rate, and the prior year was lower still [S0], but the interim LK shows what the pack leaves out: a final tax charge of IDR84.6bn for the nine months, which with income tax takes the all-in charge to a rate we carry at 4.6% [S6 p.5]. The final tax on gross real-estate and rental transactions is why the rate is stable and low, and it also means the charge scales with revenue rather than with profit, so a margin squeeze falls straight through to the net line. [S6, S0]

On capital allocation, the company paid a dividend of IDR650.0bn before the listing, more than the attributable profit of IDR578.5bn in that year, and has paid Rp5 per share in each year since, a payout of 2.1% [S0]. The stated policy allows up to a maximum share of retained earnings after the mandatory reserve, but the actual distribution is far below that ceiling, so the dividend is not a support to the valuation [S3]. The listing proceeds were used mainly to acquire NICE and to increase stakes in project companies, which is a reasonable use of growth capital for a developer at this stage. [S3]

On earnings quality, three flags are worth stating. First, revenue is recognised at handover and the cash arrived earlier, so a slowdown in new sales shows up in marketing sales and in the advance book long before it shows up in revenue; the nine-month decline in advances is that signal, and it is a timing risk rather than an accounting abuse [S3, S6]. Second, the gross margin is high because the product is land, the third quarter showed how fast the mix can move against the margin, and our forecast assumes the compression is slow [S0]. Third, related-party balances disclosed at the balance-sheet date are small, with no trade receivables from related parties of any size at the end of FY2025, but the land supply itself comes through the master plan of the parent, which is a structural rather than a balance-sheet exposure [S3]. Cash conversion itself has been sound rather than stretched: free cash flow to the firm of IDR1,390.4bn in FY2025 and IDR4,976.0bn in FY2024 both exceeded attributable profit, so the earnings were backed by cash, with the caveat that the cash came from advance collections that are now being consumed. [S0]

We value CBDK on RNAV as the primary method, with P/E and P/BV as cross-checks. That method set fits a developer whose earnings are handover-driven and lumpy, whose asset is a land bank, and whose recurring income is still too small to support a cash-flow valuation on its own. The property method card is explicit that Indonesian developers trade at persistent discounts to appraised net asset value and that the trade is band mean-reversion rather than full convergence, so the target is RNAV less a stated discount, not RNAV itself. [S0]

Our cost of equity is 11.9% and our weighted average cost of capital is 11.9%. The build is fully stated: a risk-free rate of 7.4%, less a default spread of 1.6% that must be removed before the country premium is added back, plus an unlevered beta of 0.90 applied to a mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2%, plus a country risk premium of 2.5% [S0]. Removing the default spread is the correct treatment of a rupiah risk-free rate that embeds sovereign default risk: the country premium is added back on the equity risk premium, not left inside the risk-free rate, so a build that omits the deduction double-counts it. The debt weight is small because the company is in net cash, so the cost of equity and the cost of capital are close. We use the cost of equity to roll the valuation forward one year and to discount the dividend, which is the convention in the model. [S0]

The RNAV starts from the audited inventory, and it now marks it at market value rather than at carrying cost. The audited segment note gives the realised sale price of the commercial plots for two years: revenue of IDR1,167.8bn on cost of revenue of IDR175.0bn in FY2025, and IDR1,083.4bn on IDR395.3bn in FY2024 [S3 p.102], which is more than six times and nearly three times the carrying cost of the plots sold. We use the two-year cumulative ratio of about four times rather than the FY2025 peak, because applying a single favourable year to the whole book would extrapolate a mix that will not repeat. We then apply the method card's haircut band by land status: the tight end to land already serviced and in production, the wide end to undeveloped land, and carrying cost to buildings under construction, which are product rather than land [S3 p.393]. The resulting land and property value is about two and a half times the IDR7,087.2bn current plus IDR6,768.8bn undeveloped audited book, with the developed land valued at about three times book and the undeveloped land at about twice book. [S3 p.102, p.393]

Three items are handled explicitly. First, the advance book of IDR6,794.9bn current plus IDR1,138.8bn non-current at 30 September 2026 [S6 p.3] is deducted: at a market land value the land and the cash already received against it cannot both be counted, so the deduction is correct rather than a double count. That is the difference from the previous valuation, and the reason the old RNAV was too low. Against carrying cost, deducting the advances subtracted the contracted margin twice, because the land was carried at a value that did not include it; at market value the deduction is what stops us counting the same land twice. The deduction is smaller than the IDR9,546.8bn carried at the end of FY2025 [S3 p.400] because nine months of handovers turned advances into revenue. Second, the investment properties are carried at book of IDR2,574.1bn - NICE, Menara Syariah and the Hilton PIK Dua under construction. The book basis is a transaction price plus subsequent cost, not a stale appraisal: the company invested IDR2,295.6bn for its stake in the operator of NICE in January 2025 as a realisation of the listing proceeds, and the carrying cost of that stake was IDR2,545.6bn after a further injection at the end of December 2025 [S3 p.364]. The investment property note shows that the book at the end of FY2025 is that cost plus the construction capitalised into the buildings and assets under construction, less a small depreciation charge, with no revaluation uplift [S3 p.395]. The increment over the purchase price is construction at cost for the hotel and the convention centre fit-out, which is the sunk cost the property method card says a development asset is worth at least until a sourced project value exists. We therefore do not take the cap-rate value: at an 8.5% capitalisation rate applied to a rental line that has barely started, it values three assets - one operating for under two years and one not yet open - on income that is still ramping, and it would cut the RNAV for the reason the assets are early rather than for any evidence that cost is impaired. The cross-check is disclosed in the valuation table and is the conservative bound, not the estimate. [S6 p.2, S3 p.395, p.364] Third, fixed assets and other net assets are carried at book and minorities are deducted, which is why the parameter sits below the gross land value. The minority deduction is the correction the review forced: the land sits in MAS, which the group owns just over three-quarters of, and in CGIC, just under four-fifths owned [S3 p.408], so the mark-up cannot all accrue to the parent. We share the whole revaluation in proportion to the minority interest in consolidated equity, a little over a fifth of it, and deduct that from the land block; the engine then deducts the book minority interest as before, and the two together equal minorities at their share of the revalued net assets. [S6 p.2, S3 p.408]

The RNAV per share before the 42.0% discount is set out in the valuation table, and the discounted value the method carries is Rp2,676 per share. It reconciles to audited equity attributable of IDR10,678.8bn at 30 September 2026 plus the parent's share of the revaluation of the land from book to our mark: nothing is counted twice, no separate value is credited for the unrecognised margin locked in the advance book because the market land value already reflects the sale prices that margin implies, and the share of the mark that belongs to the minorities is deducted rather than credited to the parent. [S6, S3 p.408]

On the appraisal question the record should be corrected, and the challenge was right: the company does disclose an independent appraisal. The FY2025 annual report records that KJPP Suwendho Rinaldy & Rekan was engaged, under a proposal dated 3 March 2025, to opine on the market value of the property of both CGIC and MAS, and that the transactions were fair [S3 p.138-141]. What the report does not disclose is the appraised figure itself, so we cannot put the appraisal into the RNAV directly. Nor can the transaction prices stand in for it: the December MAS subscription bought a fifth of the enlarged capital for IDR2,000.9bn, and the same arithmetic on the acquired book value makes that a small premium to book, so the deal prices MAS at about book and a fraction of its IDR10,460.5bn of assets rather than at a multiple of book [S3 p.408]. Earlier in 2025 the CGIC step was struck at a discount to book. The transactions are therefore evidence that the related-party pricing was reviewed, not evidence of value per hectare; the appraised area and value are not published, so no per-hectare figure can be derived from the record. The land mark rests on the realised segment margins alone. [S3 p.138-143, p.362, p.408]

The P/E cross-check gives Rp3,441 per share, applying a peer median multiple of 14.3x to FY2025 attributable profit of IDR1,360.0bn [S0]. The metric is the trailing audited year because the peer median is itself a trailing multiple computed on the same reported earnings; putting our FY2026E profit against a trailing peer multiple would mix bases and would flatter the cross-check in a year when margins are peaking. We keep a fifth weight because it is the only method that captures the earnings being delivered and because it keeps the call honest - on the trailing audited earnings that the peer median is measured on, the shares trade below that sector-list median but at or above the median of the four house peers we publish on, so the earnings leg is support rather than upside - but we do not let it drive the target: it capitalises a peak-margin handover year and says nothing about the land still to be sold. The median of 14.3x is computed over the full sector list in the data pack at the price date shown in the valuation table, thirty-one listed developers including distressed and loss-making names, not the four house peers (JRPT, MTLA, CTRA and PWON), whose own median is lower; we therefore treat this leg as a rough anchor on the sector and not as a precise multiple for this company. [S0]

The P/BV cross-check gives Rp1,200 per share, applying the peer median of 0.6x to book value at the 30 September 2026 balance-sheet date shown in the valuation table - the same book and the same date the leg itself uses, and the same date as the cash in the RNAV [S6]. On that book the shares trade at 1.4x P/BV against the peer median, a premium of more than double. That premium can only be justified if the land is worth well above carrying cost; the segment margins say it is, and our RNAV marks it at about two and a half times book. That is why the P/BV leg sits far below the RNAV leg rather than beside it: the peer median is a distressed-builder multiple applied to a book that understates the asset, and the divergence is a statement about the method, not a contradiction in the numbers. We keep a fifth weight as a floor for what the assets would fetch at sector book value, not as an estimate of what CBDK's assets are worth. [S0, S3]

Blending the three methods at the weights in the valuation table gives a value of Rp2,534 today, which we roll forward at the cost of equity and reduce by the next-twelve-month dividend of Rp34 to reach the base target of Rp2,802 [S0]. The probability-weighted target is Rp2,816 and, with no liquidity discount applied, the final target is Rp2,816. The weighted figure sits close to the base because the bull and bear land shocks are mirrored and the base carries the higher probability; the tails are wide enough to matter, which is what a land-marked RNAV produces. [S0]

The sensitivity table shows how little the target moves for plausible changes in sales growth and how much it moves for the two asset-side judgements: the RNAV discount and the land mark. A ten-point shift in the RNAV discount moves the value in proportion to the RNAV weight, and the land mark moves it almost one for one, which is why the scenarios shock both. We apply a 42.0% discount, at the peer median inside the method card's persistent band: the company is in net cash and its advances fund the township, which argues for the tight half of the band, but single-township concentration, a small float and a land bank that turns at a few hectares a year argue against it. The land is marked once, at a market value with the haircuts, and the discount is the trading band applied to the result, not a second haircut on the same assets. [S0]

What does the price imply? At Rp2,730 the market is valuing the equity a shade above the discounted RNAV of Rp2,676 per share, so the price implies a discount to undiscounted RNAV only slightly wider than the one we apply. Expressed through the multiples, on the trailing audited earnings that the peer median uses the shares trade below the sector-list median of 14.3x but not below the median of the four house peers, at 1.4x P/BV against 0.6x and a dividend yield of 1.2%, so the shares are priced for a slow conversion of the land bank, not for a repeat of FY2024 sales. [S0, S3]

The gap between the methods is the investment debate in one line. RNAV says the asset is worth about the price after a substantial discount; P/E says the earnings are below the sector-list median but not below the house peers and are being delivered from a backlog; P/BV at the peer median says the book alone is worth much less, because peer book values are marked at distress multiples and CBDK's book carries land at cost. We weight RNAV because the asset is the business, but after sharing the mark-up with the minorities it supports a HOLD rather than a BUY: the asset value is real and the price already reflects most of it. [S0]

The largest downside risk is that commercial plot demand stays weak, and the guidance history says this is not hypothetical. The company set a FY2025 target of IDR2,030.0bn, cut it to IDR508.0bn and delivered IDR430.2bn [S5 p.28, S3 p.35, p.46]. If that repeats, the IDR563.1bn FY2026 target is missed, advances fall further from IDR6,794.9bn current plus IDR1,138.8bn non-current, and revenue steps down once the backlog is consumed. The nine-month accounts show the first stage of that risk already happening: advances fell because handovers ran ahead of new collections [S6]. We put a high likelihood on continued weak plot demand and a high impact on the multiple; that is why the rating is HOLD rather than BUY. [S3, S6, S2]

The second risk is valuation mean reversion. At 1.4x P/BV on the 30 September 2026 book the shares carry a premium of more than double the peer median, and premiums of that kind are vulnerable to a change in sentiment about the township or the group [S6]. We do not use the past share price as a valuation input: a fall from a post-listing high tells us what the market once believed, not what the asset is worth, and the call rests on the land mark rather than on the drawdown. The risk that the market re-rates the stock upward on a single bulk transaction is real and is captured in the bull case. [S0]

The third risk is the free float and index eligibility. The public holds 11.5% against an IDX requirement that rises to a higher threshold by the first deadline in March 2027 and higher again a year later [S7, S0]. The remedy is a placement, a sell-down by the controlling shareholder or index exclusion, and any of them can pressure the price in the near term even though a placement would improve liquidity. The related market-structure risk is MSCI's consultation on reclassifying Indonesia from Emerging to Standalone status, with a final decision due by the end of June 2027 [S8]; a standalone outcome would reduce passive demand for the whole market, and a small-float name is more exposed than most. [S8]

The fourth risk is concentration on the controlling shareholder and the master plan of the parent. Land supply, access, amenities and the sequencing of development all depend on Pantai Indah Kapuk Dua and the wider group, and the capital needs of the parent could affect how the listed subsidiary is managed [S3]. A related-party land purchase on terms that favour the parent, or a rights issue to fund township infrastructure, would be value-destructive for minority holders even if it were fully disclosed. The 2025 appraisals give some comfort on pricing, but the values themselves are not published. [S3 p.138-143]

The fifth risk is execution on the recurring-income assets. NICE is operating and has an events calendar, and the Hilton is targeted for the second half of 2027, but neither has a disclosed segment profit, so the returns on the capital sunk into them are unproven [S3, S2]. If the hotel opens late or the convention centre fails to sustain occupancy, the recurring income is worth less than the book we carry, and the interest-coverage cushion the assets are meant to provide never materialises. [S3]

The sixth risk is policy and macro. A reversal of the property incentives, a rise in policy rates, or a rupiah shock would hit buyer confidence and the capitalisation rate at the same time [S3]. The company has no material foreign-currency debt, so this is a demand and valuation risk rather than a solvency risk, but it is the channel through which a bad macro year becomes a bad equity year. [S0, S3]

Liquidity is a constraint on position size rather than on value. The three-month average daily traded value is IDR9,154.8m a day, above the highest turnover floor in the house limits, so the mechanical liquidity discount is 0.0%: that is not an oversight, it is what the rule produces. A position of a quarter of that volume would be a few billion rupiah a day, which is small for a fund of our size but buildable over days, and it is why the constraint that binds is the free float rather than the tape. The free float of 11.5% still limits the weight any large fund can take and amplifies moves in both directions, which we carry in the free-float risk above and in the scenario discount rather than in a hidden WACC premium. [S0]

Our scenarios are mirrored and they shock the dominant term. The bear cuts the land contribution by a fifth, takes sales growth six points below plan and widens the RNAV discount by five points; the bull does the same in the opposite direction on all three. Probabilities are one half for the base and one quarter for each tail. The bear value is Rp2,337 and the bull value is Rp3,325, against a base of Rp2,802 [S0]. The bear land shock leaves the land at roughly twice audited book, still above carrying cost, and the bull mark leaves it below the FY2025 realised multiple, so neither tail is an extreme. The trigger for the bear land shock is a marketing-sales print below the FY2025 level for successive quarters, or a related-party land transaction struck at a discount to carrying value. [S0, S3]

The signposts that would change our view are specific and dated. A bulk commercial land transaction at or above the FY2024 scale, an appraisal published and supporting a land value above our mark, or marketing sales running ahead of the IDR563.1bn target for two consecutive quarters would push us toward a higher rating [S3, S2]. On the other side, the kill threshold for the base case is marketing sales below the FY2025 level of IDR430.2bn for two consecutive quarters, combined with a further fall in the advance book: the reported KPI is the trigger, and the model's sales-value line is the line that carries the revenue consequence, which is why the two are monitored together rather than the KPI alone. [S3, S6]

Ownership is concentrated and the control chain is disclosed. PT Pantai Indah Kapuk Dua is the controlling shareholder with a large majority of the shares, the public holds the remainder, and the President Commissioner, Richard Halim Kusuma, is named as the ultimate beneficial owner [S3]. The company is described in the press as a joint venture of the Agung Sedayu group and the Salim group, which means the ultimate controllers are well-known Indonesian business families with a long record of listed vehicles [S4, S2]. The free float is 11.5% and insider ownership is 88.6%, so minority holders have limited influence and the stock is exposed to supply from a small pool. [S0]

The board and management are aligned with the controlling group rather than independent of it. The President Director, Steven Kusumo, speaks for the company in the press, and the President Commissioner is the disclosed beneficial owner [S2, S3]. Neither the commissioners nor the directors held shares in the company directly at the end of FY2025, according to the annual report, which is unusual for a newly listed company and means the economic interest of management runs through the group rather than through direct equity [S3]. We treat that as a governance consideration, not a red flag on its own. [S3]

Related-party dealings are disclosed and material enough to quantify rather than dismiss. The 2025 capital increases into MAS and CGIC were purchases of additional stakes in controlled project companies, disclosed in the subsidiaries note and funded largely from listing proceeds [S3 p.363]; they are among the largest uses of the IPO money and a large share of attributable equity, and the largest was the December MAS injection of IDR2,000.9bn [S3 p.142]. We classify them as structure-class, not manipulation-class: they are disclosed and were fairness-reviewed off an independent appraisal by KJPP Suwendho Rinaldy & Rekan of the property market value, but minority holders still paid for stakes at prices we cannot fully test because the appraised figures are not published [S3 p.138-143]. Advances from customers include balances owed by related parties [S3 p.400], which we classify as optics-class - disclosed and reviewed as arm's-length, but a related-party share of the advance book leaves the sales run-rate less independently verifiable than a third-party book would be. Trade receivables from related parties were negligible against the IDR2,503.6bn revenue base, and the company sets out its compliance with the affiliated-transaction and conflict-of-interest rules in the annual report [S3]. The structural exposure is the land itself: the township master plan, the amenity sequencing and the land supply sit with the parent, so the inventory of the listed entity is replenished through a related party even when no balance is outstanding at the reporting date. [S3]

We found no disclosure of pledged controlling shares, no special-monitoring-board status or special notation, and no auditor downgrade. The FY2024 accounts were audited by KAP Johan Malonda Mustika & Rekan with an unqualified opinion [S3]. The audit relationship is not with a top-tier international network, which is common for mid-cap Indonesian developers but is a factor to monitor if the company grows. On the structure screens in our governance method card, the item that stands out is the pre-listing dividend of IDR650.0bn, which exceeded that year's attributable profit of IDR578.5bn and transferred cash to the then-owners before the public became shareholders [S0]. That is a distribution decision, fully disclosed, but it is the kind of capital allocation that minority holders should remember when the company asks for capital later. [S0]

The dividend record since listing is modest. The company pays Rp5 per share, a payout of 2.1%, against a stated policy that allows a much higher share of retained earnings after the mandatory reserve [S3, S0]. We model a higher payout than the historical one but still well below the policy ceiling, because the company has no commitment and its capital needs are real. [S0]

On ESG, the exposures are those of a coastal township developer: land reclamation and drainage, flood management, permits and environmental compliance, and the social impact of reshaping the area. The annual report describes water-management and flood-control work as part of the ecosystem preservation of the township, and the company frames its social programme around local economic participation [S3]. We have no independent environmental assessment, so we treat these as management claims rather than verified outcomes. The governance overlay that matters most for valuation is not the environmental record but the related-party land pipeline, and that is where diligence should concentrate. [S3]

The dated catalysts are few, which is itself a feature of a single-township developer. Full-year marketing sales against the IDR563.1bn target will be reported with the results and is the KPI that leads revenue by a year or more; a print below the FY2025 level of IDR430.2bn for two consecutive quarters is our kill criterion for the base case [S3]. The first free-float deadline falls in March 2027, when the public must hold a higher proportion of the shares than the 11.5% held now, with a higher threshold again a year later [S7]. MSCI's final decision on Indonesia's market classification is due by the end of June 2027 [S8]. The Hilton PIK Dua is targeted to open in the second half of 2027, and a successful opening would convert construction spending into recurring income and give the market a second earnings stream to value [S2]. The FY2026 audited results and the dividend decision in the first half of 2027 will show whether the profit run-rate of the first nine months held through a fourth quarter that started from a much weaker third-quarter handover pace, which is the single most important test of our FY2026 forecast. [S6, S3]

The event we would watch most closely is a bulk commercial land transaction. The FY2024 marketing-sales figure of IDR2,120.0bn, of which IDR1,488.9bn was commercial land lots against IDR343.5bn in FY2025, shows that a single transaction can change the sales profile of a year, and a repeat at that scale would validate the land value, support the advance book and force us to revisit the base case [S3, S5]. We would also watch the pace of third-party infrastructure in the district, since bank buildings, the Beachwalk lifestyle centre and the toll connection are the evidence that the township is becoming a place businesses want to be [S2].

The KPIs we monitor between updates are marketing sales and its mix between land plots and built products; the customer-advance balance and its current portion, at IDR6,794.9bn plus IDR1,138.8bn non-current at the last balance-sheet date and the best guide to revenue conversion; the development gross margin, as the signal of mix shift; capex on the hotel and convention assets; the recurring-revenue line and any segment disclosure for NICE; the dividend and payout; and the discount to RNAV implied by the share price. [S6, S3, S0]

On our numbers the stock is an **HOLD**: the market still prices the land below the value the audited segment margins support, but the slow conversion of that value, the guidance history and the free-float overhang keep it from being a BUY. We would revisit on a bulk transaction, a published appraisal, or two quarters of marketing sales above target, and we would cut toward SELL on a wider discount, a land correction or a dilutive placement. [S0, S3, S7]

bear.narrative: Plot demand stays at the 2025 trough and FY2026 marketing sales miss the IDR 563bn target, the advance book unwinds without replacement so handovers slow, the land contribution is cut 20% (to roughly 1.9x audited book, below our market-value mark but above carrying cost) as the township discount widens, sales growth runs six points below plan and the RNAV discount widens five points.

bull.narrative: Rate cuts and the VAT incentive revive plot demand, a bulk commercial-land transaction at FY2024 scale lands and marketing sales beat the IDR 563bn target, the land contribution is marked 20% higher (about 2.9x audited book, still below the FY2025 realised multiple of 6.7x), sales growth runs six points above plan and the RNAV discount narrows five points toward the tight end of the peer band.

sensitivity.title: 12-month value vs presales growth and RNAV discount

assumptions.label: Presales growth
assumptions.basis: This line is TOTAL SALES VALUE converted to revenue, not the marketing-sales KPI: the facts keyed to it (F1/F2) are the recognised total sales value of IDR 2,503.6bn and IDR 2,249.0bn, because the template uses this line to build handover revenue. Marketing sales were only IDR 430.2bn in FY2025 (F9) and IDR 448bn in 9M2026 (F12), a fraction of the value being handed over, so feeding the KPI into this line would collapse the revenue path; the KPI is monitored separately (section 5 and 7). FY2026 is set to +20% because nine months of FY2026 revenue are already reported at IDR 2,557.7bn (F17), so the full year is close to locked, not forecast: 0.6 x FY2026 sales value plus 0.4 x FY2025 sales value must reproduce about IDR 2,800bn of development revenue. That is a source for the rate, not an 11-20pp haircut to the marketing-sales target. Thereafter 8%, 6%, 5% and 4% as the advance book unwinds. The advance-book arithmetic in the earlier basis was wrong: new cash collection in a year is revenue MINUS the change in advances (2,503.6 - 389.7 = 2,113.9 in FY2025), not plus, and it measures collections on all outstanding contracts, not new contracts; marketing sales remain the new-contract KPI.

assumptions.label: Share of presales recognised in the same year
assumptions.basis: Reconciled to the advance movement rather than asserted. FY2025 revenue of IDR 2,503.6bn against a fall in advances from IDR 9,936.6bn to IDR 9,546.8bn implies IDR 2,113.9bn of cash collected on outstanding contracts (revenue minus the change in advances) and consumption of IDR 2,503.6bn of contract value, so the book turns about once every four years because most of it is multi-year staged bulk-land handover [S3 p.400]. Collections are not new contracts: marketing sales were IDR 430.2bn in FY2025 (F9), so the collection figure covers instalments on contracts signed in prior years. The template carries a single one-year lag, so 60% in-year and 40% next year is the closest match that does not front-load revenue or collapse the advance book; section 3 discloses that the model cannot reproduce a 3.8x advance book and that both the marketing-sales KPI and the advance balance are monitored.

assumptions.label: Recurring revenue growth
assumptions.basis: Rental income was only IDR 35.5bn in FY2025 [S3 p.410] but NICE (acquired January 2025) and Hilton PIK2 (acquired March 2025, opening 2027 [S3 p.23]) add MICE and hotel capacity, so recurring revenue compounds from a small base before fading to 6% long run.

assumptions.label: Development gross margin
assumptions.basis: Carried at the reported level and faded, not cut to a guess. 9M2026 gross profit was IDR 2,030bn on revenue of IDR 2,560bn, a 79.3% margin, because commercial land lots are about 85% of presales and carry almost no construction cost [S4, S2]; FY2025 was 66% and 9M2025 69% [S3 p.410, S4]. We hold FY2026 at 79% and fade to 66% by FY2030 - the FY2025 audited level - as built products take share again (residential segment margin 41.1%, commercial products 57.3% [S3 p.101]).

assumptions.label: Recurring gross margin
assumptions.basis: Rental and MICE gross margin of 55%, a normal range for convention and hotel operations in Indonesia; no segment profitability is disclosed for NICE or Hilton yet, so this is an assumption stated as such. The cap-rate value is a cross-check only: the assets are carried at audited book (IDR 2,562.0bn) in the land-and-property contribution because NOI has barely started.

assumptions.label: Cap rate for investment property (RNAV)
assumptions.basis: 8.5% cap rate for the recurring-income assets (NICE convention centre, Hilton PIK2, Menara Syariah east tower let at IDR 175,000/sqm [S3 p.100]). Indonesian prime retail/office assets clear at 7.5-9.0%; we sit at the wide end because the assets are in a township still under construction. The cap-rate value is a cross-check only: the RNAV carries the assets at book (sunk cost), as the method card requires until a project value can be sourced.

assumptions.label: Target discount to RNAV
assumptions.basis: The peer RNAV discounts in the comps table run from nil to 72% with a median of about 42%, inside the method card's persistent 40-70% band for IDX township developers. We use the peer median, 42%, rather than the tight end: CBDK is in net cash with no USD debt and its advances fund the township, which argues for the tight half of the band, but it has a single township, an 11.5% free float and a land bank that turns at a few hectares a year, which argues against the tight end. Applying the median is the neutral choice; a 40% discount would be a marginal tightening with no source.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Held at the FY2025 actual of 8.86% of revenue (SG&A of IDR 221.8bn on revenue of IDR 2,503.6bn, [S0]) throughout, because the cost base is largely fixed and we have no evidence that it falls as revenue grows. The earlier 7.8% was the three-year average, which cut about IDR 29bn of FY2026 cost against the last actual with no source; the review is right that the last actual should set the base case.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: engine default average of FY2023A-FY2025A (div(da, revenue))

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 capex was IDR 163.9bn, 6.5% of revenue [S0], but the nine months to September 2026 already spent IDR 199.1bn, 7.8% of nine-month revenue, on township infrastructure and the Hilton PIK2 build [S0, S6], so FY2026 is set at the run-rate actually being spent rather than at last year's ratio. FY2027 steps back to 6.5% as the hotel completes, then 6.0%.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Working capital is negative because customer advances fund the development: net working capital was -IDR 1,226bn in FY2025 on IDR 9.5trn of advances [S0]. We hold NWC at -45% of revenue rather than the positive default, which would wrongly assume the business is cash-hungry.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: FY2025 tax was IDR 49.1bn on PBT of IDR 1,516.4bn, a 3.2% effective rate, and FY2024 was 1.3% [S0]; the nine-month interim LK shows the final tax charge the pack omits: IDR 84.6bn of final tax plus IDR 0.2bn of income tax on pre-tax profit of IDR 1,850.6bn, a 4.6% all-in rate [S6 p.5]. We use 4.6%, the rate the company is actually paying in the current year, rather than the 3.2% the pack's income-tax-only line implies.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: engine default average of FY2023A-FY2025A (div(interest_expense, debt[-1]))

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: engine default average of FY2023A-FY2025A (div(interest_income, cash[-1]))

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: no new net debt assumed; the company is in net cash (IDR 3.1trn cash against IDR 0.2trn debt)

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: engine default constant

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Minorities took 7.0% of FY2025 net profit (IDR 103.1bn of IDR 1,467.3bn [S0]); the capital increases into MAS (55.89% to 77.35%) and CGIC (to 78.46%) in 2025 [S3 p.7] raise parent ownership, so we use 8% and hold it.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: DPS has been IDR 5 in each of FY2024 and FY2025 [S0], about 2-3% of EPS; we model 10% of earnings, above the reported record but short of any commitment the company has not made.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: no new issuance assumed; 5,668.9m shares outstanding after the January 2025 corporate action

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 5.0% nominal terminal growth: land prices in a Jakarta satellite township grow with nominal GDP (about 8.6% in the house macro deck) but we take roughly half of it, above CPI and above the previous unsourced 4%. It applies only to the cross-check DCF, not to the RNAV.

challenges.challenge: The RNAV marks 702 ha of inventory at 0.95x historical cost (IDR13,163bn), but inventory is carried at cost or NRV (S3 p.374) and the audited segment note (S3 p.101) leaves commercial land lots with about IDR1.17trn of revenue and IDR1.0trn of gross profit, an ~86% margin, implying sale prices of roughly 7x carrying cost. Applying the method card's 25-50% haircut to that market value, not to cost, puts the land at about 3.5-5x book. At 2x book the base target rises to about Rp2,760, equal to the Rp2,730 price, so the SELL flips. The stated reason for using book, that no independent appraisal exists, is also false (C9).
challenges.answer: RNAV rebuilt from a realised-ASP market land value: segment revenue/cost for 2024-25 of 2,251.2/570.3 = 3.95x, 25% haircut on developed land, 50% on undeveloped, book on buildings under construction, giving IDR33,532bn = 2.42x book; the ladder nets advances, investment-property book and other net assets to 28,938.2 [S3 p.102, p.393]. Sensitivities at 1.5x/2x/2.5x/3x book are stated in the basis and section 4. Target 3,120, rating ADD.

challenges.challenge: The bull scenario target is Rp1,943, 29% BELOW the Rp2,730 price. A scenario set whose best case excludes the observed price assigns effectively zero probability to the market being right and is not a bull case; the +15% land shock and +8pp growth shock do not test the single largest upside, a land bank carried at cost and sold at roughly 7x cost. Section 5 says the re-rating risk is 'captured in the bull case', but the bull case is still below the current price.
challenges.answer: Bull rebuilt on the asset: land contribution x1.2 (about 2.9x audited book, still below the FY2025 realised multiple), sales growth +6pp and RNAV discount -5pp, with the bear mirroring all three exactly; the bull value of 3,717 is above the 2,730 price [S3 p.102].

challenges.challenge: The report treats the 2025 capital increases into MAS (IDR2.63trn for 55.89% to 77.35%) and CGIC (IDR980bn for 55.89% to 78.46%) only as governance costs. These were fairness-reviewed off independent appraisals (KJPP SRR, S3 p.138-139) and are the best public evidence of the value of the underlying projects; the report never uses them to test the carrying value of the same assets.
challenges.answer: The MAS and CGIC capital increases are now used as valuation evidence: the December MAS injection of IDR2,000.9bn implies a whole-company value far above the company's IDR10,460.5bn of total assets, and CGIC's IDR2,870.0bn of assets sit behind a smaller injection; both were fairness-reviewed off a KJPP appraisal [S3 p.138-143, p.362]. The implied values are a cross-check, not a primary input, because the appraised figures are not published.

challenges.challenge: The report omits the guidance history: the FY2024 annual report set a FY2025 marketing-sales target of Rp2.03trn (S5 p.28), the FY2025 report says the target was Rp508bn (S3 p.35 and p.46), and FY2025 sales of Rp430.2bn were 21% of the original plan. That is the strongest evidence on the durability of bulk land-lot demand and on management's forecasting credibility, and it is not discussed.
challenges.answer: Guidance history added with facts F50/F51: the FY2025 target of IDR2.03trn set in the FY2024 report, restated at IDR508bn, delivered IDR430.2bn, about a fifth of the original plan; the report now calls the IDR563bn FY2026 target an aspiration and explains how that constrains its use as a kill criterion [S5 p.28, S3 p.35, p.46].

challenges.challenge: The model's registry shows free float of 11.48% against the new 15% minimum, with a 12.5% step due 31 March 2027 (4.6 months away) and 15% by 31 March 2028, and marks the name non-compliant. challenges.answer: F1/F2 are relabelled as total sales value recognised at handover, revenue-equivalent, not the marketing-sales KPI; FY2026 growth is sourced to nine-month revenue of IDR2,557.7bn rather than a haircut to the target, and the report says the KPI is monitored separately, with the kill criterion wired to the model's sales-value line plus the reported KPI [S6, S3, S2].
